name: avx-ecm
baseline: GMP-ECM (the ecm program, built on GMP)
workload: Elliptic Curve Method factoring: curves per second for stage 1 and stage 2 on general inputs up to about 1000 bits, AVX-512 8-way (52-bit digits) or 16-way (32-bit digits) vector arithmetic per thread.
claimed_speedup: about 1.5 to 2.5 times the throughput (curves/sec) of GMP-ECM, for numbers up to a thousand bits or so (README, 'has been observed'). README adds that large numbers are more efficient with GMP-ECM because AVX-ECM does not use sub-quadratic multiplication.
compiler_and_flags: README names only gcc 7.3.0 or newer and icc, built with 'make COMPILER=gcc730 SKYLAKEX=1' (ICELAKE=1 or TIGERLAKE=1 for IFMA, KNL=1 for Knights Landing); no benchmark flags for the quoted ratio.
tradeoffs: Needs AVX-512 (Skylake-X, Knights Landing, or IFMA on Ice Lake/Tiger Lake). Curves run in constant-time steps of 208 bits (128 bits with DIGITBITS=32), so 417-bit and 623-bit inputs cost the same. No sub-quadratic multiplier, so it loses to GMP-ECM on large inputs. Stage 2 is the standard continuation with pairing (B2 = 100 x B1 by default). It writes a stage 1 savefile that GMP-ECM stage 2 can resume. Multi-threaded with pthreads. Not a library: command-line program.
caveats: README ratio is a first-party 'has been observed' range with no table, CPU model, GMP-ECM version or flags, and no benchmark script in the README. The mersenneforum thread (www.mersenneforum.org is blocked here) was seen only as a search snippet, which says about 2x GMP-ECM throughput with 1 thread on a Xeon Gold 5122 and, for one input size, 16 simultaneous 512-bit curves in 18.7 s (1.17 s/curve) versus GMP-ECM at 1.72 s/curve (ratio about 1.47, derived from snippet data); the snippet could not be opened, so treat those as unverified. The comparator is GMP-ECM, not GMP itself, so it only loosely matches the listed GMP/MPFR baselines. Last commit 2021-03-09 (repo inactive for over 5 years). Newer GMP-ECM releases and AVX-512 downclocking were not measured.

name: metal-flash-attention
baseline: Dao-AILab FlashAttention-2 (A100) and FlashAttention-3 (H100), compared by utilization percentage, not wall time
workload: Single-headed attention forward, backward dQ and backward dK/dV kernels in FP16 on Apple GPUs (M1 Max, M4, M3 architecture) at head dimensions D = 64, 128, 256, measured as gigainstructions per second and ALU utilization against a hardware roofline.
claimed_speedup: No wall-clock ratio against any other library. README: a consistent 4400 gigainstructions per second on M1 Max (83% ALU utilization) at infinite sequence length and head dimension with BF16 emulation. Forward utilization on M1 architecture 86% (D=64), 85% (D=128), 86% (D=256); forward + backward 62%, 63%, 64%. M3 architecture forward 94%, 91%, 82%; forward + backward 71%, 69%, 61%. Quoted comparison tables: A100 Flash2 FP16 forward + backward 56% (D=64), 65% (D=128), 0% (D=256, no result reported); H100 Flash3 FP16 forward + backward 48%, 59%, 0%. README claims 'Apple hardware is training transformers faster than Nvidia hardware doing the same work' after normalizing for GPU size and utilization.
compiler_and_flags: swift build/test with -Xswiftc -Ounchecked (README); Metal kernels are JIT compiled at runtime.
hardware: Apple M1 Max (roofline 10616 GFLOPS, 5308 gigainstructions/s), M4 (3580 GFLOPS); NVIDIA A100 SXM and H100 SXM figures are taken from the FlashAttention papers, not re-measured.
stars_or_usage: 612 stars; a Draw Things blog post and the derived mps-flash-attention project build on it
tradeoffs: Single-headed attention only (no multi-head, masks or block sparsity yet). Backward pass avoids FP32 atomics by using 7 GEMMs instead of 5 (9D+15 versus 7D+10 work per N^2), which uses less memory than the official backward pass but more compute. Intentional register spilling with a third blocking dimension along D for large head dimensions. Needs Apple silicon and Swift/Metal; JIT compiles shaders at runtime. Not a drop-in C++ or Python library.
caveats: The listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor) are not compared. The only comparison is utilization against FlashAttention-2 and FlashAttention-3 on different hardware, using the author's own metric (gigainstructions, with the NVIDIA side converted from the papers' best reported GFLOPS divided by peak). It is not a speed comparison and cannot show Apple hardware is faster in wall time. README raw data is in a Google Sheet that was not opened. I found no comparison of this repo against MLX, MPS or PyTorch MPS attention in the README or in search results. The separate project imperatormk/mps-flash-attention (opened; credits this repo) claims 1.1-2.0x (1024), 1.7-3.7x (2048), 2.0-3.9x (4096), 3-4x (8192+) faster than PyTorch SDPA, average 1.8x, on 'Apple Silicon M1-M5', and its search snippet gives 5.3 ms versus 15 ms for N=2048, B=4, H=8, D=64 on M1 Max; that is a derived project and not evidence for this repo. The deepwiki and Medium pages were blocked. Last commit 2024-09-22.

name: avxbls
workload: Full optimal ate pairing on BLS12-381 (Miller loop plus final exponentiation), single pairing latency in CPU cycles, AVX-512 IFMA 52-bit limb arithmetic versus blst's mulx/adx scalar assembly.
claimed_speedup: Per the TCHES 2025(4):848-872 paper (abstract seen as a search snippet only): 1,265,314 cycles (Granger-Scott cyclotomic squaring) or 1,195,236 cycles (compressed cyclotomic squaring) for the full pairing versus blst at 2,351,615 cycles, i.e. blst is 1.86x (resp. 1.97x) slower.
compiler_and_flags: Repo Makefile: gcc -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -m64 -mbmi2 -march=native -fwrapv -mtune=native -z noexecstack; test and bench binaries built with -DTEST and -DBENCHMARK. Cycle counts use read_tsc via src/rdtsc64.S, 10000 iterations after cache warm-up (src/main.c timing_pairing). gcc version not stated in the repo.
hardware: Intel Core i3-1005G1 (Ice Lake) per the paper abstract snippet; the repo itself does not state the CPU.
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 with IFMA (Ice Lake or newer Intel, Zen 4/5 class AMD with IFMA). Latency-optimized for a single pairing, not aggregate batch throughput. Built on and bundles blst sources (a baseline directory carries the scalar reference). The repo is pairing only; signatures are in a separate project.
caveats: The paper is not in the repo (the root has README, Makefile, LICENSE, baseline, bin, hybridmul, src) and the paper pages (tches.iacr.org, eprint.iacr.org, researchgate) are blocked here, so the cycle counts and CPU come from a WebSearch snippet of the abstract and were not opened on a page. The repo's bench code (src/main.c, make bench) is public, and a baseline directory holds a blst-based scalar build, so a verifier with paper access can raise this to A. Cycle counts on one laptop-class CPU; AVX-512 frequency effects and wall-clock time are not reported in the snippet. Baseline is blst, not GMP or MPFR, so it is outside the listed baselines. The final commit date is just over 12 months old.

name: NICSLU open source (wibraun/NICSLU, v3.0.1)
baseline: SuiteSparse KLU (also PARDISO, SuperLU, UMFPACK in the authors' papers)
workload: Sparse LU factorization of circuit-simulation matrices (left-looking Gilbert-Peierls with MC64 static pivoting, parallel and re-factorization modes); no benchmark in this repo.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in this repo, its README or the bundled doc/ug.pdf user guide (dated 2013-08-27). Papers by the NICSLU authors report speedups over KLU, but they were not opened (see caveats).
compiler_and_flags: README: gcc with -O2, 'CANNOT be -O3'; macros SSE2, NICS_INT64, NO_EXTENSION, NO_ATOMIC in make.inc.
stars_or_usage: 10 stars, 8 forks, 6 commits; third-party mirror of NICSLU 3.0.1 by wibraun (original code Copyright 2011-2013 Tsinghua University, by Xiaoming Chen)
tradeoffs: C library, x86/x86-64 only (SSE2 hand-optimized paths), Windows or Linux. Does not use BLAS and is aimed at extremely sparse circuit matrices; supports repeated factorization with the same nonzero pattern. Sequential and multi-threaded demos (demos, demop).
caveats: Licensing is mixed: the library is LGPL-2.1, but source/nicslu_mc64.c and nicslu_mc64scale.c are HSL MC64 code whose terms (open issue #1 'MC64 conditions on external use', opened 2018-12-11) require attribution, forbid giving the code to third parties without the HSL authors' prior consent, and may go beyond the LGPL. The lead says the original author's FAQ calls this version old and buggy; I could not open that FAQ (the author site was not tried and nicsefc.ee.tsinghua.edu.cn is blocked), so that remark is unverified. A WebSearch snippet attributes to the NICSLU paper a geometric-mean speedup of 2.08x to 8.57x over KLU with 1-12 threads on matrices suitable for the parallel algorithm, and says its factorization with pivoting scales to only about 2x on 8-16 threads; the paper PDF (DATE15_23.pdf) was blocked, the paper may describe a later NICSLU than 3.0.1, and these numbers are unverified. Newer solvers (CKTSO, GLU3.0, ISLU) are reported to beat NICSLU. The closed-source NICSLU is already catalogued separately. Last commit 2018-09-04.

name: ranluxpp-portable
baseline: std::ranlux48 (RANLUX, the generator RANLUX++ reimplements; the README states no baseline)
workload: Generating 1e9 64-bit values from RANLUX++ (576-bit LCG state, p=2048) with ./ranluxpp-test -n 1e9.
claimed_speedup: README: RANLUX++ runs at 1.4 GiB/s on a Core i7-8650U @ 1.90GHz, and 1e9 64-bit values take 7.7 seconds. No comparison against std::ranlux48, mt19937 or xoshiro in the repo.
tradeoffs: Standalone C port (no assembly, no AVX2 requirement, uses 128-bit multiplication) of Sibidanov's RANLUX++, combining it with the ROOT C++ portable implementation. Quality is RANLUX-class (long-period, high statistical quality, built for Monte Carlo) rather than mt19937/xoshiro-class speed. Includes a SHA-256 and reference-output check for p=2048, seed=1, and an optional GMP-based 576-bit arithmetic test.
caveats: No numeric comparison against any recognizable baseline, so tier D; the repo has 0 stars and is only a seed-list entry. Do not read this as faster than mt19937 or xoshiro: the ROOT blog (opened via github.com/root-project/web, AMD Ryzen 9 3900, GCC 8.3.1) puts ROOT's tuned portable RANLUX++ at about 9 ns per number, Sibidanov's assembly at about 8 ns, TRandom1 (RANLUX) at about 62 ns and TRandom3 (Mersenne Twister) at about 3 ns, so RANLUX++ beats RANLUX but not Mersenne Twister; those figures are for other implementations, not this repo. Sibidanov's README (opened via raw.githubusercontent.com) claims 20 clock/float versus 198 clock/float for the GCC C++ RANLUX at Haswell, for the original assembly code. Repo figures for this port: 7.7 s per 1e9 values is about 7.7 ns per 64-bit value (derived from page data). The Hahnfeld-Moneta paper (arXiv 2106.02504, cds.cern.ch) was blocked. Library files are under the ROOT LGPL-2.1-or-later terms (LICENSE), while ranluxpp-test.c carries a GPL-3.0-or-later header. Last commit 2021-06-22.
